{"rule":"Return this JSON object with the rule field unchanged and a new passage of about 250 words in the text field.","text":"On the morning the river ran backward, Tomas was carrying a basket of apples to the market. He stopped on the bridge and watched the water climb toward the hills, lifting leaves and forgotten twigs as easily as a breeze might carry feathers.

At the riverbank, a girl in a yellow coat was trying to catch a wooden boat. It drifted upstream, its little sail stitched from a blue handkerchief. Tomas set down his basket and reached over the railing, but the boat slipped past his fingers.

“Follow it,” the girl called. “It knows where it’s going.”

They hurried along the path. The boat wound through reeds and under an old stone arch, then turned into a narrow channel Tomas had never noticed. At its end stood a cottage with a crooked chimney. An elderly woman waited outside, holding a matching wooden boat in her hands.

The girl ran to her. “I told you it would come back.”

The woman smiled, though her eyes were wet. She explained that her brother had carved the boats when they were children. He had gone away many years ago, and the river had carried his little boat downstream the day before he left.

Tomas looked at the water. It was already flowing toward the sea again, as if nothing unusual had happened. The woman placed the returned boat beside its twin on the windowsill.

When Tomas reached the market, his apples were gone. In their place lay a smooth river stone, warm as a pocketed coin. He kept it, and whenever the current seemed to carry something away, he remembered that some things find their way home."}
